_note: Phase F content, written during D because the guide's later beats need something to hang on. Schema from docs/ip-plan-v2.md: { id, kind, title, beats[], needs[] }. kind is main | side | egg | depth. needs[] names line ids that must be complete first, and a gate only exists where the lesson genuinely depends on the earlier one.
_caveat: 240.0.0.0/4 has been reserved since RFC 791, 1981-09, and our own registry confirms it is unallocated - so the line about it is true today. There is a live IETF effort to redesignate it as usable unicast space. If that lands, the line needs rewriting rather than deleting: it becomes a better fact, not a dead one.
_verified: Every fixed address below was checked on 2026-09-18 against apps/ip/data/space.bin - the file this app actually ships - not against an external source. Two claims died in that check and are not in here: 18.0.0.0 is dated 1994 in our registry, not the 1977 the published /8 lists give, so no line claims 1977; and our data carries no holder names at all, so no line names an organisation. Holders arrive from the live lookup and the plate says them. Where a beat needs routing data we do not ship, it is a find[] rule the engine resolves rather than an address I asserted.
_beats: at = a fixed address, verified. find = a rule the sightline engine resolves at runtime, so the chain works without me knowing the answer. say = the guide. teaches = why the beat exists; it is never shown.

lines.title: Where you actually are
lines._note: Reconciles two lists that were never the same list: the seven beats in ip-plan-v2.md say what each step TEACHES, and the eight in ip-emotional-design.md say what each step FEELS. Teaching without a feeling is a curriculum; a feeling without a fact is a caption. Each beat below carries one of each, and the emotional beat is named so a later session cannot quietly drop it.
lines._reframe: Beats 6 and 8 share one sentence VERBATIM - 'Every network decides for itself what to believe' - and it is the only deliberate repetition in the product. At 6 it is the reason nothing is guaranteed. At 8, after the hijack, it is the reason anything works. Nothing new is added; the floor tilts. Edit one and you must edit the other or the ending stops working.
lines._ending: Four words. The emotional design says the bigger the moment the fewer his words, and that the best paragraph at the climax is the failure mode. The flare, the ring and the descent tone stopping carry the rest.

beats.teaches: it is a number, and somebody agreed to it
beats.say: There. It exists somewhere other than here now, which is more than most of this map can say.

beats.find: the prefix the visitor's address is announced in
beats.teaches: somebody speaks for you
beats.say: Somebody stands up and says this range is theirs to speak for, and you are inside it. You have never met them.

beats.find: another prefix the same network announces
beats.teaches: a network is not one range
beats.say: Same network, different part of the map entirely. A network is not a place. It is a list of ranges somebody is willing to answer for.

beats.find: the whole of the visitor's address family
beats.teaches: the size, and how little of it is left
beats.say: All of it. Every number there will ever be in this family, and nearly all of them are taken. It still carried everything you did today.

beats.find: the whole of the visitor's address family
beats.teaches: the size, and how little of it has been needed
beats.say: All of it. Vastly more than has ever been handed out, and the part in use is a rounding error against the rest.

beats.teaches: a handful of named things hold the rest up, and people looked after them by hand
beats.say: Thirteen names hold up every name there is. And for years the register of which numbers had been given to whom was published, and largely kept, by one man.

beats.find: the origin network of any announced prefix
beats.teaches: announcing is a claim, and every listener decides what to do with it
beats.say: A network can announce anything it likes. Every network decides for itself what to believe. Some of that is checked now - not all of it, and none of it was then.

beats.teaches: a claim meant for one country escaped
beats.say: In 2008 a route meant to block one site inside one country escaped. For about two hours it pulled that site's traffic across the internet to somewhere it was never going. No one meant that to happen, which is the part worth sitting with.

beats.find: the whole of the visitor's address family, again
beats.teaches: the same fact, read the other way
beats.say: Every network decides for itself what to believe. And mostly, they agree.

lines.reveal: No single authority tells any network which route to trust. Each one accepts, rejects or checks what it hears, and most of the time those decisions agree well enough to have carried everything you did today.
lines._verified: 208.65.153.0 is present in space.bin as ARIN / US / 2006. The 2008 incident is sourced in docs/ip-story-research.md; RIPE's own analysis states it could not determine how many sites were affected, so the beat says traffic was pulled across the internet and does NOT claim universal failure. 'Some of that is checked now' is deliberately unquantified - origin validation is real, widely deployed and nowhere near universal, and any number would be wrong within a year.

lines.title: The boundary
lines.provisional: Needs the inward half - phase H - which does not exist. The beats are written so the spine is settled and the side chains have something to point at, but nothing here can be built or locked yet.
lines._note: The plan's beats 6 and 7. The instrument turns around, and the product ends where it should. Fear appeal is the cheapest win available here and taking it would make this a worse product: show how little was kept and let the relief be the payoff.

beats.find: what actually crossed the wire to get here
beats.teaches: what a visit really reveals
beats.say: Everything I have shown you came from one number and a handful of public registers. Here is all of it.

beats.teaches: your address is not you
beats.say: This is where I stop being able to see. Your address says where to send the answer. It does not say who you are, and I could not tell you.

lines.reveal: An address is a delivery instruction that a great many strangers have agreed to honour. That is all it is, and it is not nothing.

lines.title: The oldest hands
lines._verified: 1982 is the earliest year present in space.bin. 12.0.0.0/8 is dated 1983 and is a whole /8. 9.0.0.0/8 is dated 1988.

beats.teaches: the record goes back further than people expect
beats.say: Nineteen eighty-two. There is nothing older in the register I carry.

beats.teaches: early allocations were enormous and casual
beats.say: Sixteen million addresses, to one organisation, in one go. The year after the oldest record there is.

beats.teaches: it kept happening for a decade
beats.say: And again. They were not being careless. There was no reason yet to be careful.

lines.reveal: For about ten years the internet was small enough that you could give away sixteen million addresses without anyone needing to think about it.

lines.title: Set aside
lines._verified: All three are landmarks already in MARKS and are RFC facts, not lookups. On the date, which is contested: RFC 791 (1981-09) defined the class E range as reserved, while the IANA special-purpose registry records 1989-08 for its own entry. Those are two different events. The landmark line names 1981, which is the reservation rather than the registry record, and this chain names no date at all. Our own space.bin independently shows the range unallocated.

beats.teaches: space can be reserved and then never arrive
beats.say: A sixteenth of the whole space, kept back for an addressing idea that never arrived. Nobody has ever been given any of it.

beats.teaches: some addresses exist so that writing can be safe
beats.say: This one exists so that writing about addresses cannot accidentally name a real one.

beats.teaches: the same idea, made much larger the second time
beats.say: And the same again in IPv6, with room for every example anyone will ever need.

lines.reveal: Some of this space was never meant for the public internet. Kept back for an addressing idea, or handed to writing so examples cannot collide with anything real. Different reasons, same result: a place on the map that nobody is going to.

lines.title: The thirteen
lines._verified: Root addresses come from the IANA root hints, already in MARKS, both families.

beats.teaches: there is a first one and it is an ordinary-looking address
beats.say: A. There is nothing about this address that looks like what it does.

beats.teaches: they are separated by operator and site, not by address
beats.say: E. Different people, different buildings, different networks from the last one. That is the part that matters, not where they sit on this map.

beats.find: the same letter in the other family
beats.teaches: the thirteen exist twice
beats.say: And the same letter again, in the other internet. Thirteen is not thirteen machines.

lines.reveal: Thirteen letters hold up every name on the internet, and the number is small enough that people argue about it.

lines.title: Sold, and given back
lines._verified: 36.0.0.0 reads APNIC / CN / 2011 in space.bin, which is consistent with the block having been returned and reissued. 18.0.0.0 reads ARIN / US / 1994. No holder is named by any line here; the plate names them from the live lookup.

beats.teaches: a founding-era /8, and what happened to it is visible rather than asserted
beats.say: One of the big early ones. Look at who announces the halves of it now, and then look again.

beats.teaches: the opposite decision, and the register records the consequence
beats.say: This one is registered on the other side of the world now, to a registry that did not exist when it was first handed out.

lines.reveal: Once there was no more of it, address space became something you could transfer. Where a block is registered today and where it started are two different questions, and this map only answers the first.
lines.provisional: The RETURN is not verified. space.bin shows 36.0.0.0 registered to CN under APNIC in 2011, which is consistent with a block having been given back and reissued and is not evidence that it was. Either a real historical source arrives or this chain does not ship. The beats are written so it can be decided rather than forgotten.

lines.title: Small countries, old space
lines._verified: Computed from space.bin 2026-09-18: Singapore holds 27,894,080 v4 addresses of which 66.0% were allocated before 1993, the highest share of any country holding over a million. North Korea holds one range of 1,024 addresses.

beats.teaches: share of old space has nothing to do with size
beats.say: Two thirds of this was handed out before 1993. Of every country holding more than a million addresses, none has a larger share that old.

beats.teaches: the other end of the same scale
beats.say: One range. A thousand addresses, for a country.

lines.reveal: How much of this is registered to a country says almost nothing about how large the country is, and a great deal about how early the people asking for it got there.

lines.title: The quiet ones
lines._note: Half authored, half computed - the template from docs/ip-story-research.md. The engine supplies the addresses because we cannot know them in advance; only the meaning is written.

beats.find: allocated before 2000, and nothing announces it
beats.teaches: old and silent is a real and common state
beats.say: Somebody was given this before the century turned. There is no route to it that I can see today.

beats.teaches: it is not a one-off
beats.say: Another. They are not rare, once you know the shape of them.

beats.find: the largest run of them nearby
beats.teaches: the dark is not empty
beats.say: All of this is registered to somebody. None of it answers right now.

lines.reveal: Allocated a long time ago, and no route to any of it that anyone here can see today. That is all this shows, and it is enough: the dark on this map is not empty space. It is held space that has gone quiet, and there is far more of it than anybody expects.

lines.title: Where the map is wrong
lines._note: Gated for a real reason, not an arbitrary one: a block announced from the wrong continent is not STRANGE until you have watched an ordinary network's footprint stay where it was put. Entirely computed - it needs live routing data we do not ship.

beats.find: a prefix whose registered country differs from the country its origin network is registered under
beats.teaches: the register records paperwork, not geography
beats.say: Registered under one country. Announced by a network registered under another. Neither of them is lying.

beats.find: a second one, in a different registry
beats.teaches: it is structural, not an error
beats.say: Again, and nothing is wrong. This is what the two records are for.

lines.reveal: One record says which country the paperwork was filed under. The other says which network is announcing it. People read the first as a map of where the machines are, and it was never that - and this is two records disagreeing, not a measurement of anywhere.
